title: Two cousins, two big bets: Will the Lopez split actually work?
summary: The real test of a family divorce begins after the relatives sign their agreements

blocks.text: PART 1 | Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach usPART 2 | Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?

The Ambani brothers got what they wanted in 2005: the freedom to run their businesses without having to answer to each other. Their mother, Kokilaben, helped divide the Reliance empire founded by their father, Dhirubhai Ambani. Mukesh, the elder brother, took control of the oil, petrochemicals, and refining businesses. Anil, the younger, received interests in telecommunications, power, and financial services.

More than two decades later, the brothers’ business fortunes could hardly be more different. Mukesh built Reliance Industries into one of India’s largest companies, expanding into telecommunications through Jio and consumer businesses through Reliance Retail. Anil’s business empire, once valued in the billions of dollars, suffered heavy debts, corporate insolvencies, and the collapse of some of its most prominent enterprises. Both brothers gained independence, but only one turned that freedom into a sustained expansion.

That 20-year history offers a sobering preview for Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III, Federico “Piki” Lopez, and the other third generation heirs now unbundling their own family family empire in the Philippines. Following Gabby’s P11.56-billion exit from Lopez Inc. in August, Piki’s September board consolidation at Lopez Holdings and FPH, and FPH’s November approval to sell Rockwell Land to Gabby’s Crème Investment Corp. for almost P16 billion, the Lopezes are moving toward separate corporate spheres. (Click these links below for the author’s special reports on these developments:
Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled itPart 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN strugglesPart 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

The cousins are not dividing their group in the exact same way the Ambanis did, nor is their separation complete. Yet the questions hanging over both families are remarkably similar: Will the businesses become stronger when the relatives no longer have to agree on how they should be run? Will the separation end the fighting? And what happens to the shareholders, employees, and younger heirs who must live with the consequences?
The real test of a family divorce begins after the relatives sign their agreements.

The first two installments of this series examined why business families fight, whether they should stay together or separate, and how they can negotiate a division of their interests. This final installment looks at what happened to families that went through the process years earlier.
After all, the real test of a family divorce begins after the relatives sign their agreements.

The Ambanis offer one of the clearest long-term tests of a family-business separation because enough time has passed to examine what each brother did with the businesses he controlled. In the financial year ending March 2026, Reliance Industries reported consolidated revenue of ₹11.76 trillion and profit after tax of about ₹95,754 crore. Its telecommunications business served more than 524 million subscribers, while its retail operations had grown to more than 20,000 stores. Mukesh had not merely preserved the oil and petrochemicals businesses he inherited, he had used their financial strength to build major new businesses in industries that barely figured in the family’s original empire.

Anil’s experience was very different. Reliance Communications, once a major competitor in India’s telecommunications industry, entered insolvency proceedings after accumulating debts it could not service. The company became subject to a court-supervised resolution process, and Anil resigned from its board in 2019. Other businesses associated with his group also underwent financial difficulties and restructuring. The Reliance Group even emphasized that Reliance Communications is no longer under Anil’s management and that its remaining operating companies should be assessed separately.

It would be convenient to conclude that Mukesh made the right choices and Anil made the wrong ones. But that would oversimplify what happened. Telecommunications changed dramatically as competition intensified, particularly after Mukesh’s Jio entered the market in 2016. Financing decisions, accumulated debt, industry regulation, and the timing of investments all influenced the brothers’ fortunes. The 2005 division gave them freedom to make those decisions. It did not determine how those decisions would turn out.

There is also another question: Did the separation actually end their disputes? Not entirely. The brothers subsequently fought over the supply and pricing of natural gas, a disagreement that reached India’s Supreme Court. Their businesses were separate, but they still had commercial interests that brought them into conflict. Later reports of Mukesh helping Anil meet a financial obligation suggested that the relationship was more complicated than an unbroken feud, although such episodes cannot establish the state of their private relationship.

The Ambanis’ experience illustrates the difference between settling a family dispute and succeeding in business afterward. The brothers gained control of their respective enterprises. What they accomplished with that control was another matter.

The Bajaj family’s experience reinforces the point. The division of its business interests gave different branches greater independence, but the companies that emerged from the arrangement did not enjoy identical fortunes.

Bajaj Auto has become one of India’s major motorcycle and three-wheeler manufacturers. In the financial year ending March 2026, it reported record standalone revenue of ₹58,732 crore and profit after tax of ₹9,825 crore, an increase of more than 20% from the previous year. The wider Bajaj financial-services businesses have also expanded significantly. Bajaj Finance reported assets under management exceeding ₹5 trillion in the same financial year.

Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar, associated with Shishir Bajaj’s branch, experienced a more difficult period. Its 2026 annual report described financial pressures arising from high sugarcane procurement costs, relatively flat sugar prices, and difficulties servicing debt. The company reported a loss of ₹751 crore for the previous financial year before returning to a reported profit of about ₹138 crore in the year ending March 2026. Its November 2026 financial disclosures continued to discuss restructuring arrangements and the need to manage liquidity.

The difference is striking, but it is not proof that the Bajaj separation benefited one branch at the expense of another. Motorcycles, financial services, and sugar are very different businesses. They face different markets, regulatory requirements, and operating risks. Sugar producers in India, for example, are affected by government policies governing cane prices and sugar sales, factors that have little to do with disagreements among shareholders.

What the Bajaj experience does demonstrate is that once relatives gain control of their respective businesses, their fortunes increasingly depend on the companies they manage and the industries in which they operate.
The separation may have settled who controlled the businesses, but it did not guarantee how those businesses would perform.
Not every family dispute ends with relatives dividing an entire conglomerate. Sometimes independence means leaving the management of a business while building another enterprise.

Walter Kwok, the eldest of three brothers who inherited Hong Kong property developer Sun Hung Kai Properties, lost his leadership position following a prolonged dispute with his brothers. He subsequently established Empire Group Holdings, pursuing property development outside the company his father had founded.

Walter died in 2018, but Empire continued operating. The privately held company has undertaken residential, commercial, and hospitality developments, demonstrating that Walter established a substantial business outside Sun Hung Kai. That does not establish whether he became wealthier than he would have been had he remained in charge of the family company.

But his experience illustrates something important about family-business disputes: ownership, management, and independence are not necessarily the same thing. A family member may lose the right to run a company without losing all financial interests in it. Another may choose to surrender a position in an established enterprise to pursue opportunities elsewhere.
The question is not always who gets to keep the family company. It can also be whether the relatives are better able to pursue their ambitions without constantly contesting control.
There is another measure of success that cannot be found in a company’s financial statements: whether the relatives themselves are able to move beyond the conflict.

The Ambani brothers’ dispute over natural gas showed that dividing ownership does not necessarily eliminate commercial disagreements. Even after companies have been separated, relatives may remain connected through contracts, investments, obligations, and the history of decisions made when the businesses were still together.

Other family disputes have demonstrated how difficult it can be to separate corporate disagreements from personal relationships. In the Philippines, the Ilusorio family’s conflict extended into disputes over family authority and the care of elderly parents. The Yanson family’s disagreement over the Vallacar Transit group involved competing claims to management and ownership that produced years of legal proceedings. Those histories were discussed in Part 1 and 2 of this series.

But a separation need not restore close personal relationships to succeed as a business arrangement. Relatives who can no longer work together may prefer to run their businesses independently and maintain a more distant personal relationship. That may be preferable than remaining partners in an enterprise where every major decision becomes another family confrontation.
Corporate peace, however, should not be confused with family peace.

The distinction becomes especially important when the relatives belong to a family whose businesses have been associated with its identity for generations. Disagreements over corporate control can become disagreements over legacy: who deserves to lead, whose contribution matters most, and who has the right to decide what happens to the assets accumulated by parents and grandparents.
A separation may reduce the occasions for corporate disagreement. Whether it changes the relationships among relatives is a different question.
A family settlement can be satisfactory to the relatives who negotiated it and still create problems for their children.

The Ambani family’s experience offers an opportunity to examine the next stage. Mukesh’s children—Isha, Akash, and Anant—have assumed increasingly prominent responsibilities in the Reliance businesses. Akash chairs Reliance Jio Infocomm, Isha has played a leading role in retail, and Anant has taken on responsibilities in the group’s energy and other businesses. The family’s succession arrangements are being developed within the enterprise Mukesh expanded after the 2005 separation.

That development is significant because the original division did more than establish which brother controlled which assets. It created separate business structures within which their descendants would eventually exercise ownership and management responsibilities.

The Bajaj family offers another example of business interests passing to younger generations after an earlier division. But a clear separation among branches does not automatically resolve every future succession question. Children and grandchildren may eventually disagree among themselves over who should manage a company, how profits should be distributed, or whether particular assets should be sold.

Family-business advisers Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer have written about how family feuds can threaten businesses when money, authority, and personal relationships become intertwined. Their work is a useful reminder that removing one source of conflict does not necessarily eliminate the conditions that produced it.

Asian family business adviser Enrique Soriano makes a related point about inheritance: He argued that passing ownership to the next generation does not necessarily mean passing on a business capable of functioning successfully under its new owners. Inheriting shares and being equipped to manage a company are different matters. His point raises another way of judging family settlements: Should success be measured by what the relatives accomplish immediately after separating, or by what happens when their children and grandchildren take over? (READ: If great business dynasties can fracture, why would your family be any different?)

For the Lopezes, that question may be answered only 10 or 20 years from now. Their younger heirs will inherit not only the businesses that Gabby, Piki, and their third generation cousins choose to retain, but also the ownership arrangements, financial obligations, and family relationships left by the current dispute. Whether those arrangements prove durable may ultimately be a more meaningful measure of success than the agreements reached today.
The longer-term test of a family settlement may therefore come when the next generation begins exercising the ownership and leadership rights established by their parents.

When business families fight, the headlines usually focus on the relatives: who controls the company, who gets the assets, and how much each branch receives. But the consequences extend to people who did not participate in the dispute and have little influence over its outcome.

Reliance Communications’ insolvency left creditors dealing with a court-supervised resolution process. Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar’s financial difficulties required negotiations with lenders over debt and liquidity. Neither company’s difficulties can simply be blamed on its family’s earlier separation. They nevertheless demonstrate that the financial decisions of controlling shareholders and managers can have consequences far beyond their own fortunes.

For the Lopez group, the changes have also been felt in its boardrooms and executive offices. Long-serving executives have left positions they held for years, while changes in shareholdings have brought new directors and altered the composition of boards. One significant departure was Salvador Tirona. He had worked with the Lopezes since early 2000s-and served as president, chief operating officer, and chief finance officer of Lopez Holdings. At the September 14 annual meeting, Piki’s brother Jay Lopez took over Tirona’s executive positions. Tirona also resigned from ABS-CBN Holdings, where he had served as chairman and held senior executive posts.

Another longtime corporate officer, Enrique Quiason, resigned as corporate secretary of First Philippine Holdings in November after nearly 34 years with the company. Both Tirona and Quiason resigned—not retired—during a period of major changes in ownership and leadership, although neither cited the family feud as the reason for leaving.

Earlier, when the cousins were exchanging increasingly hostile public statements, two independent directors of Lopez Holdings also stepped down. Roberto Panlilio resigned effective May 1, followed by Consuelo Garcia on May 5. Both cited personal reasons. Their departures left the seven-member board with only one independent director at the time.

The family conflict was also being discussed directly with employees. At a First Gen town hall on April 17, Piki acknowledged the dispute but urged employees not to become involved in choosing between the warring relatives. “There’s no need for you to take sides,” he said. He described the fight as a shareholder conflict that would eventually work itself out. His message was to remain professional and continue doing their jobs.

At ABS-CBN, employees received a more difficult message. During a September 15 town hall, president and CEO Carlo Katigbak announced another round of retrenchments—around 200 employees, or 7% of its workforce—even as the company was preparing to receive P6 billion in fresh capital from the Lopez family and other investors. Katigbak told employees that this would be the last retrenchment program under his leadership, but it followed years of job cuts since ABS-CBN lost its broadcast franchise in 2020, when about 5,000 employees were retrenched.

blocks.caption: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way

blocks.text: The contrast between the new investments and the latest job losses was difficult to ignore. The additional capital was intended to help ABS-CBN recover, but it did not remove the need to reduce expenses. In its September statement, the company cited weak advertising and consumer spending, inflation, and difficult conditions in the content industry.

The retrenchments cannot be solely attributed to the bitter Lopez family feud. ABS-CBN’s financial difficulties began years before the cousins’ dispute became public. But the layoffs demonstrate why the outcome of the family’s business decisions matters to people outside the family. For employees, a successful turnaround is not simply a stronger balance sheet or the arrival of new investors. It is a company capable of sustaining jobs and paying the people who work for it. (READ: Banks, retirees, the business: Where will ABS-CBN’s P6-billion rescue go?)

Creditors have their own concerns. ABS-CBN must demonstrate that it can generate enough cash to meet its obligations, including loans that may require refinancing or extensions. Banks will have to assess whether the company’s recovery plans provide a credible basis for continued lending.

Minority shareholders also have a stake in what happens next. Rockwell’s public shareholders face a proposed change in control. FPH’s November disclosure states that the transaction requires, among other conditions, a mandatory tender offer by Crème to other Rockwell shareholders. The terms of that offer will matter to investors who did not participate in the family’s negotiations.

For employees, the test is whether the businesses can sustain jobs. For creditors, it is whether debts are repaid. For minority shareholders, it is whether their investments are protected and rewarded.
These interests do not always coincide with those of the relatives negotiating a settlement. They cannot be left out when judging whether a corporate divorce worked.

The experiences of the Ambanis and Bajajs bring us back to the Lopezes. Their separations gave different family branches the freedom to pursue their own business strategies. But the results depended on what businesses they controlled, the investments they made, the risks they took, and their ability to finance those decisions.

For Federico “Piki” Lopez, the future increasingly depends on energy. His group is committing enormous resources to renewable power and infrastructure projects that may take years to complete and even longer to recover their investment costs.

Geothermal energy, pumped-storage hydropower, and other large projects require substantial capital upfront. They involve technical studies, regulatory approvals, financing, construction, and agreements for selling the electricity they will eventually produce. Delays can increase costs, while changes in electricity prices and financing conditions can affect returns.

The Lopez group has decades of experience in the power business. But experience does not remove the risks of committing large amounts of capital to projects whose expected earnings lie years, if not decades, ahead.

The question is whether Piki is making the right investments now to secure substantial earnings years from today. Will the projects produce enough cash to justify their cost? Can the group finance the years of development without taking on excessive debt? And will selling Rockwell, an established property business, prove a worthwhile exchange for the capital needed to pursue those ambitions?

FPH has told the stock exchange that selling Rockwell would allow it to redirect resources toward energy, infrastructure, and other businesses where it sees opportunities. The proposed transaction would bring in nearly P16 billion, but the amount of cash raised is only one measure of its value. The more important test is what FPH eventually earns from the investments it makes with that money.

blocks.text: For Gabby Lopez and the majority cousins, the challenge is almost the opposite. They are committing resources to ABS-CBN at a time when the economics of the media industry are being rewritten.

Before losing its franchise, ABS-CBN produced television programs and distributed them through its own nationwide broadcast network. It controlled much of the process, from creating shows to delivering them to viewers and selling advertising around those audiences. Today, ABS-CBN remains a content producer but relies on broadcast partners, streaming services, and digital platforms to reach audiences. It must negotiate distribution arrangements, compete for attention across multiple platforms, and find ways to earn enough from its content in a market where viewers and advertisers have more choices. (READ: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study)

The P6-billion capital infusion may provide breathing room, but it cannot by itself establish a profitable business model. Can ABS-CBN consistently earn more from its content than it spends producing and distributing it? Can it control costs without sacrificing the talent and production capabilities that remain its principal strengths? And can it generate sufficient cash to meet its obligations rather than depend on repeated financial support?

blocks.caption: Industry disruption continues: GMA’s profit falls 98% in Q3, ABS-CBN still in red

blocks.text: The proposed acquisition of Rockwell adds another dimension to Gabby’s bet. Rockwell has established assets and earnings, but acquiring it requires substantial capital. Its cash flows must first support its own operations, development projects, financing requirements, and shareholders. How much, if anything, could eventually be available to support the other investments of Gabby’s branch?

Nor should Rockwell’s profits automatically be treated as money available to ABS-CBN. The two companies have different shareholders, creditors, and financial obligations. Rockwell’s ability to distribute cash to its owners depends on its own financial condition and corporate requirements. Whether Gabby’s branch can use such distributions to support ABS-CBN will also depend on how the Rockwell acquisition is financed and which entities receive the dividends.
That brings both sides to a question that rarely features prominently in accounts of family feuds: Will their bankers continue to have confidence in them?

Piki’s group must finance projects whose expected returns lie years ahead. Gabby’s branch must manage the cost of a major acquisition while supporting a media business still searching for sustainable profitability.

For ABS-CBN, the debt question is particularly pressing. Its ability to meet repayment schedules, refinance obligations, and retain access to bank credit will depend partly on whether its operating performance improves.

Extending loan maturities can be a normal part of corporate financing. But when a business repeatedly needs more time because it cannot generate enough cash to meet its obligations, lenders must reassess the risks.

The relevant questions are not simply how much debt ABS-CBN owes, but when its loans fall due, how much interest it must pay, whether its operations generate enough cash, and what security or guarantees its lenders hold. Those obligations must also be distinguished from any financing arrangements used by Crème or other companies to acquire Rockwell.

Banks have their own reasons for supporting companies through difficult periods. They may prefer a workable restructuring to an immediate default. But their willingness to extend credit is not unlimited. A turnaround must eventually demonstrate that the borrower can repay what it owes.
The separation may give each cousin greater control over the businesses he believes in. It also makes the consequences of those choices more clearly his responsibility.
The Lopezes may eventually discover what the Ambanis learned after their own division: freedom to pursue a business strategy and success in carrying it out are two very different things.

blocks.caption: The secret to the Lopez family’s enduring control of ABS-CBN

blocks.text: The experiences of other families offer no guarantee that the Lopez separation will work. The Ambanis demonstrate that independence can produce dramatically different business fortunes. The Bajajs show that the industries and financial circumstances inherited by each branch matter enormously. Walter Kwok’s experience shows that leaving an established family enterprise need not mean the end of a business career.

None of these examples proves that separation is always preferable to remaining together. They demonstrate that settling ownership is one achievement. Making the resulting businesses successful is another.

For the Lopezes, the immediate questions concern whether the proposed transactions are completed and whether the new ownership arrangements establish more stable control. But the harder questions will take much longer to answer.

Will Piki’s large investments in energy generate the returns needed to justify their cost? Can Gabby’s branch build a sustainable future for ABS-CBN in an industry whose business model is still changing? Will Rockwell prove a valuable investment without becoming an excessive financial burden? And can both sides generate enough cash to repay creditors, finance their ambitions, and reward shareholders?
And when the next generation takes over, will it inherit companies capable of prospering under the arrangements made today—or another set of disputes over ownership and control?

A family settlement can end the argument over who owns what and who gets to run the business. It cannot guarantee that the companies will prosper, that the relatives will reconcile, or that their children will be spared another fight.

For the Lopezes, the separation may finally give each branch greater freedom to pursue its own ambitions. Whether that freedom produces stronger businesses, healthier relationships, and a better future for the next generation will take years to discover. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.
